In [[mathematics]], in particular [[abstract algebra]] and [[topology]], a '''homotopy Lie algebra''' (or '''<math>L_\infty</math>-algebra''') is a generalisation of the concept of a [[differential graded Lie algebra]]. To be a little more specific, the [[Jacobi identity]] only holds up to homotopy. Therefore, a differential graded Lie algebra can be seen as a homotopy Lie algebra where the Jacobi identity holds on the nose. These homotopy algebras are useful in classifying deformation problems over characteristic 0 in [[Deformation (mathematics)|deformation theory]] because [[deformation functors]] are classified by [[quasi-isomorphism]] classes of '''<math>L_\infty</math>'''-algebras.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Lurie|first=Jacob|author-link=Jacob Lurie|url=http://people.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/papers/DAG-X.pdf|title=Derived Algebraic Geometry X: Formal Moduli Problems|page=31, Theorem 2.0.2}}</ref> This was later extended to all characteristics by Jonathan Pridham.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Pridham|first=Jonathan Paul|year=2012|title=Derived deformations of schemes|url=http://www.intlpress.com/site/pub/pages/journals/items/cag/content/vols/0020/0003/a004/|journal=Communications in Analysis and Geometry|volume=20|issue=3|pages=529–563|doi=10.4310/CAG.2012.v20.n3.a4|arxiv=0908.1963|mr=2974205}}</ref>

Homotopy Lie algebras have applications within mathematics and [[mathematical physics]]; they are linked, for instance, to the [[Batalin–Vilkovisky formalism]] much like differential graded Lie algebras are.

== Definition ==
There exists several different definitions of a homotopy Lie algebra, some particularly suited to certain situations more than others. The most traditional definition is via symmetric multi-linear maps, but there also exists a more succinct geometric definition using the language of [[formal geometry]]. Here the blanket assumption that the underlying field is of [[Characteristic (algebra)|characteristic zero]] is made.

===Geometric definition===
A '''homotopy Lie algebra''' on a [[graded vector space]] <math>V = \bigoplus V_i </math> is a continuous derivation, <math>m</math>, of order <math> >1 </math> that squares to zero on the formal manifold <math>\hat{S}\Sigma V^*</math>. Here <math>\hat{S}</math> is the completed [[symmetric algebra]], <math>\Sigma</math> is the suspension of a graded vector space, and <math>V^*</math> denotes the linear dual. Typically one describes <math>(V,m)</math> as the homotopy Lie algebra and <math>\hat{S}\Sigma V^*</math> with the differential <math>m</math> as its representing commutative differential graded algebra.

Using this definition of a homotopy Lie algebra, one defines a morphism of homotopy Lie algebras, <math>f\colon(V,m_V)\to (W,m_W)</math>, as a morphism <math>f\colon\hat{S}\Sigma V^*\to\hat{S}\Sigma W^*</math> of their representing commutative differential graded algebras that commutes with the [[vector field]], i.e., <math>f \circ m_V = m_W \circ f </math>. Homotopy Lie algebras and their morphisms define a [[category (mathematics)|category]].

===Definition via multi-linear maps===
The more traditional definition of a homotopy Lie algebra is through an infinite collection of symmetric multi-linear maps that is sometimes referred to as the definition via higher brackets. It should be stated that the two definitions are equivalent.

A '''homotopy Lie algebra'''<ref name=Daily04/> on a [[graded vector space]] <math>V = \bigoplus V_i </math> is a collection of symmetric multi-linear maps <math>l_n \colon V^{\otimes n}\to V</math> of degree <math>n-2</math>, sometimes called the <math>n</math>-ary bracket, for each <math>n\in\N</math>. Moreover, the maps <math>l_n</math> satisfy the generalised Jacobi identity:
:<math> \sum_{i+j=n+1} \sum_{\sigma\in \mathrm{UnShuff}(i,n-i)}  \chi (\sigma ,v_1 ,\dots ,v_n ) (-1)^{i(j-1)} l_j (l_i (v_{\sigma (1)} , \dots ,v_{\sigma (i)}),v_{\sigma (i+1)}, \dots ,v_{\sigma (n)})=0,</math>
for each n. Here the inner sum runs over <math>(i,j)</math>-unshuffles and <math>\chi </math> is the signature of the permutation. The above formula have meaningful interpretations for low values of <math>n</math>; for instance, when <math>n=1</math> it is saying that <math>l_1</math> squares to zero (i.e., it is a differential on <math>V</math>), when <math>n=2</math> it is saying that <math>l_1</math> is a derivation of <math>l_2</math>, and when <math>n=3</math> it is saying that <math>l_2</math> satisfies the Jacobi identity up to an exact term of <math>l_3</math> (i.e., it holds up to homotopy). Notice that when the higher brackets <math>l_n</math> for <math>n\geq 3</math> vanish, the definition of a [[differential graded Lie algebra]] on <math>V</math> is recovered.

Using the approach via multi-linear maps, a morphism of homotopy Lie algebras can be defined by a collection of symmetric multi-linear maps <math>f_n\colon V^{\otimes n} \to W</math> which satisfy certain conditions.

===Definition via operads===
There also exists a more abstract definition of a homotopy algebra using the theory of [[operad]]s: that is, a homotopy Lie algebra is an [[algebra over an operad]] in the category of chain complexes over the <math>L_\infty</math> operad.

== (Quasi) isomorphisms and minimal models ==
A morphism of homotopy Lie algebras is said to be a (quasi) isomorphism if its linear component <math>f\colon V\to W</math> is a (quasi) isomorphism,  where the differentials of <math>V</math> and <math>W</math> are just the linear components of <math>m_V</math> and <math>m_W</math>.

An important special class of homotopy Lie algebras are the so-called '''minimal''' homotopy Lie algebras, which are characterized by the vanishing of their linear component <math>l_1</math>. This means that any quasi isomorphism of minimal homotopy Lie algebras must be an isomorphism. Any homotopy Lie algebra is quasi-isomorphic to a minimal one, which must be unique up to isomorphism and it is therefore called its '''minimal model'''.

== Examples ==
Because <math>L_\infty</math>-algebras have such a complex structure describing even simple cases can be a non-trivial task in most cases. Fortunately, there are the simple cases coming from differential graded Lie algebras and cases coming from finite dimensional examples.

=== Differential graded Lie algebras ===
One of the approachable classes of examples of <math>L_\infty</math>-algebras come from the embedding of differential graded Lie algebras into the category of <math>L_\infty</math>-algebras. This can be described by <math>l_1</math> giving the derivation, <math>l_2</math> the Lie algebra structure, and <math>l_k =0</math> for the rest of the maps.

=== Two term L<sub>∞</sub> algebras ===

==== In degrees 0 and 1 ====
One notable class of examples are <math>L_\infty</math>-algebras which only have two nonzero underlying vector spaces <math>V_0,V_1</math>. Then, cranking out the definition for <math>L_\infty</math>-algebras this means there is a linear map
:<math>d\colon V_1 \to V_0</math>,
bilinear maps
:<math>l_2\colon V_i\times V_j \to V_{i+j}</math>, where <math>0\leq i + j \leq 1</math>,
and a trilinear map
:<math>l_3\colon V_0\times V_0\times V_0 \to V_1</math>
which satisfy a host of identities.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Baez|first1=John C.|author1-link=John C. Baez|last2=Crans|first2=Alissa S.|date=2010-01-24|title=Higher-Dimensional Algebra VI: Lie 2-Algebras|journal=Theory and Applications of Categories|volume=12|pages=492–528|doi=10.70930/tac/17zgrru6 |arxiv=math/0307263}}</ref> <sup>pg 28</sup> In particular, the map <math>l_2</math> on <math>V_0\times V_0 \to V_0</math> implies it has a lie algebra structure up to a homotopy. This is given by the differential of <math>l_3</math> since the gives the <math>L_\infty</math>-algebra structure implies
:<math>dl_3(a,b,c) = -[[a,b],c] + [[a,c],b] + [a,[b,c]]</math>,
showing it is a higher Lie bracket. In fact, some authors write the maps <math>l_n</math> as <math>[-,\cdots,-]_n: V_\bullet \to V_\bullet</math>, so the previous equation could be read as
:<math>d[a,b,c]_3 = -[[a,b],c] + [[a,c],b] + [a,[b,c]]</math>,
showing that the differential of the 3-bracket gives the failure for the 2-bracket to be a Lie algebra structure. It is only a Lie algebra up to homotopy. If we took the complex <math>H_*(V_\bullet, d)</math> then <math>H_0(V_\bullet, d)</math> has a structure of a Lie algebra from the induced map of <math>[-,-]_2</math>.

==== In degrees 0 and n ====
In this case, for <math>n \geq 2</math>, there is no differential, so <math>V_0</math> is a Lie algebra on the nose, but, there is the extra data of a vector space <math>V_n</math> in degree <math>n</math> and a higher bracket
:<math>l_{n+2}\colon \bigoplus^{n+2} V_0 \to V_n.</math>
It turns out this higher bracket is in fact a higher cocyle in [[Lie algebra cohomology]]. More specifically, if we rewrite <math>V_0</math> as the Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> and <math>V_n</math> and a Lie algebra representation <math>V</math> (given by structure map <math>\rho</math>), then there is a [[bijection]] of quadruples
:<math>(\mathfrak{g}, V, \rho, l_{n+2})</math> where <math>l_{n+2}\colon \mathfrak{g}^{\otimes n+2} \to V</math> is an <math>(n+2)</math>-cocycle
and the two-term <math>L_\infty</math>-algebras with non-zero vector spaces in degrees <math>0</math> and <math>n</math>.<ref name=":0" /><sup>pg 42</sup> Note this situation is highly analogous to the relation between [[group cohomology]] and the structure of [[N-group (category theory)|n-groups]] with two non-trivial homotopy groups. For the case of term term <math>L_\infty</math>-algebras in degrees <math>0</math> and <math>1</math> there is a similar relation between Lie algebra cocycles and such higher brackets. Upon first inspection, it's not an obvious results, but it becomes clear after looking at the homology complex
:<math>H_*(V_1 \xrightarrow{d} V_0)</math>,
so the differential becomes trivial. This gives an equivalent <math>L_\infty</math>-algebra which can then be analyzed as before.

==== Example in degrees 0 and 1 ====
One simple example of a Lie-2 algebra is given by the <math>L_\infty</math>-algebra with <math>V_0= (\R^3,\times)</math> where <math>\times</math> is the cross-product of vectors and <math>V_1=\R</math> is the trivial representation. Then, there is a higher bracket <math>l_3</math> given by the [[dot product]] of vectors
:<math>l_3(a,b,c) = a\cdot (b\times c).</math>
It can be checked the differential of this <math>L_\infty</math>-algebra is always zero using basic linear algebra<ref name=":0" /><sup>pg 45</sup>.

=== Finite dimensional example ===
Coming up with simple examples for the sake of studying the nature of <math>L_\infty</math>-algebras is a complex problem. For example,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Daily|first1=Marilyn|last2=Lada|first2=Tom|date=2005|title=A finite dimensional <math>L_\infty</math> algebra example in gauge theory|url=https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.hha/1139839375|journal=[[Homology, Homotopy and Applications]]|volume=7|issue=2|pages=87–93|doi=10.4310/HHA.2005.v7.n2.a4|mr=2156308|doi-access=free}}</ref> given a graded vector space <math>V = V_0 \oplus V_1</math> where <math>V_0</math> has basis given by the vector <math>w</math> and <math>V_1</math> has the basis given by the vectors <math>v_1, v_2</math>, there is an <math>L_\infty</math>-algebra structure given by the following rules
:<math>\begin{align}
& l_1(v_1) = l_1(v_2) = w \\
& l_2(v_1\otimes v_2) = v_1, l_2(v_1\otimes w) = w \\
& l_n(v_2\otimes w^{\otimes n-1}) = C_nw \text{ for } n \geq 3
\end{align},</math>
where <math>C_n = (-1)^{n-1}(n-3)C_{n-1}, C_3 = 1</math>. Note that the first few constants are
:<math>\begin{matrix}
C_3 & C_4 & C_5 & C_6 \\
1 & -1 & -2 & 12
\end{matrix}</math>
Since <math>l_1(w)</math> should be of degree <math>-1</math>, the axioms imply that <math>l_1(w) = 0</math>. There are other similar examples for super<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Fialowski|first1=Alice|last2=Penkava|first2=Michael|year=2002|title=Examples of infinity and Lie algebras and their versal deformations|url=http://www.impan.pl/get/doi/10.4064/bc55-0-2|journal=Banach Center Publications|volume=55|pages=27–42|doi=10.4064/bc55-0-2|arxiv=math/0102140|mr=1911978|s2cid=14082754}}</ref> Lie algebras.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Fialowski|first1=Alice|last2=Penkava|first2=Michael|year=2005|title=Strongly homotopy Lie algebras of one even and two odd dimensions|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0021869304004818|journal=[[Journal of Algebra]]|volume=283|issue=1|pages=125–148|doi=10.1016/j.jalgebra.2004.08.023|arxiv=math/0308016|mr=2102075|s2cid=119142148}}</ref> Furthermore, <math>L_\infty</math> structures on graded vector spaces whose underlying vector space is two dimensional have been completely classified.<ref name="Daily04">{{Cite thesis|last=Daily|first= Marilyn Elizabeth|date=2004-04-14|title=<math>L_\infty</math> Structures on Spaces of Low Dimension |type=PhD |hdl=1840.16/5282 |url=https://repository.lib.ncsu.edu/handle/1840.16/5282}}</ref>
